topics.h: Is your home full of cousins, or is it just you and your parents? Every family is special!
p: A family is a group of people who live together, love each other and look after each other.
A small family may have only parents and their children.
A big joint family may have grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins living together.
Some children live with one parent, or with grandparents. These are loving families too.
We have special names for relatives, like dadi, nani, chacha, mama, bua and mausi.

ex.q: Kabir lives with his mother, father, dadi, dadu, chacha, chachi and two cousins. What kind of family is this?
st: Count who lives in the home: parents, grandparents, an uncle, an aunt and cousins.
Many relatives from different generations live together under one roof.
A family like this is called a joint family.
ex.a: A joint family

topics.rl: At a family wedding or a festival you may meet many relatives at once. Ask an elder to tell you how each one is related to you!

rv.summary: A family is people who live together, love and look after each other. Families can be small, big joint families, or children living with one parent or grandparents.
focus: Every kind of family is a real family
remember: Small family: parents and their children
Joint family: grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins live together
Mama = mother's brother; bua = father's sister; dadi = father's mother; nani = mother's mother
traps: Don't mix up mama (mother's brother) and chacha (father's brother).
A family does not need many people; love and care make a family.

topics.h: Dadi's stories are the best! But who helps Dadi when her knees hurt?
p: Elders are older people like grandparents. They have lots of love and lots of stories.
As people grow old, they may walk slowly, see less clearly or forget things.
We can help them: fetch their glasses, read to them, or walk slowly beside them.
Spending time and talking with elders makes them happy.
We show respect by speaking politely and listening to them.

ex.q: Nanu's glasses are in the next room and he wants to read the newspaper. What can Asha do?
st: Think: Nanu needs glasses to read, and walking is hard for him.
Asha can bring the glasses to him.
She can also offer to read the news aloud with him.
ex.a: Bring Nanu his glasses, or read the newspaper aloud to him

topics.rl: When your grandparents visit or call, tell them about your school day. They love hearing from you!

rv.summary: Elders like grandparents have lots of love and stories. As they grow old they may need help, so we help them, spend time with them and speak politely.
focus: Showing respect and staying close to elders
remember: Old age can make eyes, knees and memory weaker
Help: fetch glasses, read to them, walk slowly beside them
Respect: speak politely, greet them and listen
traps: Elders are not lazy; their bodies may become weaker.
Never take away an elder's walking stick.

topics.h: What makes a friend a good friend? Is it sharing laddoos? Maybe!
p: Friends play together, share things and help each other.
Good friends take turns, say sorry when they make a mistake and forgive each other.
Friends can be different from us. They may speak another language or like other games.
Including a new child in your game is a kind thing to do.
Friends cheer for each other and feel happy for each other.

ex.q: A new girl, Lhamo, has joined your class from Sikkim. She sits alone at lunch. What can you do?
st: Think: being new can feel lonely.
You can smile, say hello and ask her name.
Invite her to sit with your group and play at break.
ex.a: Say hello, ask her name and invite her to join you

topics.rl: At school, in the park or in your colony, a kind word can start a new friendship.

rv.summary: Friends play, share and help each other. Good friends take turns, say sorry, forgive, include new children and feel happy for each other.
focus: Making friends with children who are different
Being kind to a new child
remember: Take turns and share
Say sorry when you make a mistake, and forgive
Friends can speak other languages or like other games
traps: Friends do not have to speak the same language.
A friend who teases you all the time is not a good friend.

topics.h: Giant wheels, jalebis and balloons everywhere! Shall we go to the mela?
p: A mela is a big fair where many people come together to shop, eat and have fun.
At a mela you see rides like the giant wheel and the merry-go-round.
There are stalls selling bangles, toys, pots, clothes and tasty snacks.
Many melas are held at festival times or after the harvest.
Some melas are famous, like the Pushkar fair in Rajasthan, where camels are brought for trade.

ex.q: Tara has ₹50. A balloon costs ₹10 and a plate of jalebi costs ₹30. If she buys both, how much money is left?
st: Add the costs: ₹10 + ₹30 = ₹40.
Take it away from what she has: ₹50 − ₹40 = ₹10.
Planning before spending helps us buy what we really want.

topics.rl: Melas are held in many towns and villages. Look out for one near you at festival time, and always go with a grown-up.

rv.summary: A mela is a big fair where people shop, eat and enjoy rides. Many melas happen at festival times or after the harvest, like the Pushkar fair in Rajasthan.
focus: What you see and do at a mela
Why many melas come after the harvest
remember: Rides: giant wheel, merry-go-round
Stalls: bangles, toys, pots, clothes, snacks like jalebi
Pushkar fair (Rajasthan) is famous for camels
traps: The Pushkar fair is in Rajasthan, not Punjab or Kerala.
Kathputli string puppets come from Rajasthan.

topics.h: Who blows up all those balloons? Who makes the bangles? Let's meet the mela workers!
p: Many people work hard to make a mela fun for us.
A potter makes pots and diyas from clay.
A balloon seller, a toy seller and a bangle seller sell their goods at stalls.
Cooks fry snacks, and ride operators run the giant wheel safely.
Every kind of work is useful, and we should respect every worker.

ex.q: At the mela, Gopal sells clay pots and diyas that he made on a spinning wheel. What is his work called?
st: Think: he makes things from clay.
He shapes them on a spinning wheel.
A person who makes things from clay is a potter.
ex.a: He is a potter

topics.rl: In your neighbourhood you can see many workers too: the vegetable seller, the cobbler, the tailor and the sweeper. Thank them!

rv.summary: Many people work to make a mela fun: potters, sellers, cooks, ride operators, mehendi artists and cleaners. Every kind of work is useful, and we should respect every worker.
remember: Potter makes pots and diyas from clay
Cobbler repairs shoes and chappals
Ride operator runs the giant wheel safely
Cleaners keep the ground clean
traps: Don't think only some workers matter; every kind of work is useful.
Never take things from a stall without paying.

topics.h: A mela is fun but very crowded. What if you lose your family? Here's how to stay safe!
p: Always stay close to your grown-up and hold their hand in a crowd.
Learn your full name, your parent's name and phone number by heart.
Fix a meeting place, like the big gate, in case you get separated.
If you are lost, stay where you are or go to a help desk or a police officer.
Never go anywhere with a stranger, even if they offer sweets or toys.

ex.q: Mohan cannot find his mother at the mela. What should he do?
st: First, do not panic and do not wander far away.
Look for the help desk, a police officer or a stall owner near the meeting place.
Tell them his name and his mother's name and phone number.
ex.a: Stay calm, go to the help desk or a police officer, and share his parent's name and phone number

topics.rl: In India, 112 is the emergency number. A grown-up can call it for help anywhere.

rv.summary: In a crowd, stay close to your grown-up, know your parent's name and phone number, fix a meeting place, and never go with strangers. If lost, stay calm and go to a help desk or police officer.
focus: What to do if you get lost
remember: Hold your grown-up's hand in a crowd
Know your full name, parent's name and phone number by heart
If lost: stay calm, go to a help desk or police officer
112 = India's emergency number
traps: Never go with a stranger, even for sweets or toys.
Don't run away when lost; stop and stay calm.

topics.h: India has so many festivals that there is something to celebrate almost every month!
p: People of many religions and regions live in India, so we have many festivals.
Diwali is the festival of lights, and Holi is the festival of colours.
Eid ul-Fitr comes at the end of the month of Ramzan. Christmas is celebrated on 25 December.
Harvest festivals thank nature for crops: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Baisakhi in Punjab and Onam in Kerala.
National festivals belong to every Indian: Republic Day on 26 January, Independence Day on 15 August and Gandhi Jayanti on 2 October.

ex.q: Farmers in Tamil Nadu cook rice with milk and jaggery in a new pot to thank the Sun and the cattle for a good crop. Which festival is this?
st: The clues are: Tamil Nadu, new rice, and thanking nature for a crop.
That makes it a harvest festival of Tamil Nadu.
The festival, and the sweet rice dish too, is called Pongal.
ex.a: Pongal

topics.rl: Look at a calendar at home. Circle the festivals your family celebrates and the ones your friends celebrate!

rv.summary: India has many festivals because people of many religions and regions live here. There are festivals like Diwali, Holi, Eid and Christmas, harvest festivals, and national festivals for every Indian.
focus: Main festivals and what they are known for
remember: Diwali = festival of lights; Holi = festival of colours
Christmas = 25 December; Eid ul-Fitr = end of Ramzan
Harvest festivals: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Bihu (Assam), Baisakhi (Punjab), Onam (Kerala)
Republic Day 26 January; Independence Day 15 August; Gandhi Jayanti 2 October
traps: Don't mix up the states: Bihu is Assam, Onam is Kerala.
National festivals belong to all Indians, not one state.

topics.h: Every festival has a special smell — sweets frying, flowers, fresh paint. Let's explore festival customs!
p: Each festival has special foods. Modaks for Ganesh Chaturthi, sevaiyan for Eid and cake for Christmas.
On Makar Sankranti, people fly kites and eat sweets made of til (sesame) and gur (jaggery).
In Kerala, the Onam feast, called sadya, is served on a banana leaf.
People decorate homes with rangoli, kolam, lights or flowers, and often wear new clothes.
At a gurdwara, people of every background sit together and eat free food at the langar.

ex.q: Fatima's family is making sweet vermicelli cooked in milk and greeting neighbours with 'Eid Mubarak'. Which dish is this?
st: Vermicelli is thin noodle-like strands.
Sweet vermicelli in milk is a favourite festival dish for Eid.
It is called sevaiyan (or sheer khurma).
ex.a: Sevaiyan

topics.rl: Ask your family which special dish they make for a festival, and help them make it with an adult watching.

rv.summary: Each festival has special foods and customs, like modaks on Ganesh Chaturthi, til-gur and kites on Makar Sankranti, sadya on a banana leaf at Onam, and langar at a gurdwara.
remember: Modak – Ganesh Chaturthi; sevaiyan – Eid; cake – Christmas; gujiya – Holi
Makar Sankranti: kites and til (sesame) + gur (jaggery) sweets
Onam sadya is served on a banana leaf
Langar = free food for everyone at a gurdwara
traps: Gur means jaggery, not salt or chilli.
Rangoli and kolam are floor patterns, not mehendi.

topics.h: A festival is more fun with friends! Why do we love celebrating together?
p: Festivals bring families, friends and neighbours together.
People share sweets and greet each other, like 'Happy Diwali' or 'Eid Mubarak'.
Many of us join friends in celebrating their festivals too.
We can celebrate kindly: use natural colours on Holi and keep noise low so pets, birds and elders are not scared.
On national festivals, all of us celebrate together as Indians.

ex.q: Neha's neighbour Joseph invites her family for Christmas. Neha's family invites Joseph's family for Diwali. What does this show?
st: Both families share each other's happy days.
They learn about each other's customs.
This shows friendship and togetherness among neighbours.
ex.a: Festivals help neighbours share joy and come closer

topics.rl: Your school may celebrate many festivals together in the assembly. Each one is a chance to learn something new.

rv.summary: Festivals bring families, friends and neighbours together to share joy and food. We celebrate kindly by using natural colours, keeping noise low and cleaning up together.
focus: Celebrating in ways kind to nature, animals and elders
remember: Greetings: 'Happy Diwali', 'Eid Mubarak'
Use natural colours on Holi
Keep noise low so pets, birds and elders are not scared
National festivals are celebrated by all Indians together
traps: Loud crackers are not harmless; they scare animals and disturb babies and elders.
Don't leave litter after a party; clean up together.

topics.h: A plant is like a little factory with many parts. Each part has its own job!
p: Most plants have roots, a stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
Roots grow under the soil. They hold the plant firmly and take in water from the soil.
The stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves.
Leaves make food for the plant using sunlight, air and water.
Plants come in many sizes: tiny grass, bushy shrubs like the rose, and tall trees like the neem and banyan.

ex.q: Anu pulls a weed out of the garden. It comes out with long thin threads at the bottom, full of soil. What are these threads, and what did they do for the weed?
st: The threads were under the soil.
The part of a plant that grows under the soil is the root.
Roots hold the plant in the soil and take in water.
ex.a: They are roots. They held the weed in the soil and took in water.

topics.rl: Next time you water a pot plant, remember: the roots drink the water, and the stem carries it up to the leaves.

rv.summary: Most plants have roots, a stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. Roots hold the plant and take in water, the stem carries water up, and leaves make food. Plants can be grass, shrubs or tall trees.
focus: Sizes of plants: grass, shrub, tree
remember: Roots: hold the plant and take in water
Stem: holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves
Leaves: make food using sunlight, air and water
Tree's thick, hard stem = trunk
traps: A carrot is a root, not a stem.
A rose is a shrub, not a tree.

topics.h: Have you ever seen two leaves that look exactly alike? Leaves and flowers are full of surprises!
p: Leaves come in many shapes and sizes: the banana leaf is huge, and the tulsi leaf is small.
A leaf has a flat part, thin lines called veins, and a small stalk joining it to the stem.
Most leaves are green. Leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant.
Flowers have colourful petals and many have a sweet smell.
Bees and butterflies visit flowers. After this, many flowers grow into fruits with seeds inside.

ex.q: Rohit sees bees buzzing around the mustard flowers in the field. Later, the flowers turn into thin pods. What is happening?
st: Bees visit flowers to drink their sweet juice, called nectar.
This visit helps the flowers to make seeds.
The flowers then change into pods, which are the fruits that hold mustard seeds.
ex.a: The flowers are turning into pods (fruits) with seeds inside

topics.rl: Collect fallen leaves in your park and compare their shapes, sizes and edges. Do not pluck leaves from plants!

rv.summary: Leaves come in many shapes and sizes and have veins. Flowers have colourful petals; bees and butterflies visit them, and many flowers then grow into fruits with seeds.
focus: Which part of a plant we eat (palak, cauliflower)
remember: Veins = thin lines on a leaf
Petals = colourful parts of a flower
Bees drink nectar and make honey
Lotus grows in ponds and is India's national flower
traps: We eat the flower of the cauliflower, not its leaves.
Many flowers turn into fruits with seeds, not into new leaves.

topics.h: A giant banyan tree starts as one tiny seed. How does a seed become a plant?
p: Seeds are found inside fruits. A mango has one big seed; a papaya has many small seeds.
A seed can grow into a new plant when it gets water, air and warmth.
When a seed starts to grow, a tiny root comes out first, and then a small shoot.
Seeds travel to new places. Cotton and aak (madar) seeds fly with the wind, coconuts float on water, and birds drop seeds of fruits they eat.
We eat many seeds, like rice, wheat, dal, peas and peanuts.

ex.q: Simran soaks moong seeds in water overnight and keeps them wrapped in a wet cloth. After a day, tiny white tails appear. What has happened?
st: The seeds got water, air and warmth.
They started to grow, which we call sprouting.
The tiny white tail is the first root of the new plant.
ex.a: The seeds have sprouted. The white tail is the first root.

topics.rl: Sprouted moong is eaten as a healthy snack in many Indian homes. You can grow your own with an adult's help!

rv.summary: Seeds are found inside fruits. With water, air and warmth a seed sprouts: first a tiny root, then a shoot. Seeds travel by wind, water and animals, and we eat many seeds.
focus: What comes out first when a seed sprouts
remember: Seeds need water, air and warmth to grow
The tiny root comes out first, then the shoot
Cotton and aak fly with the wind; coconut floats; birds drop seeds
Mango has one big seed; papaya has many
traps: The leaf does not come out first; the root does.
Seeds do not need darkness or salt to grow.

topics.h: What would a cow, a parrot and a squirrel do without plants? They would be hungry and homeless!
p: Many animals eat plants. Cows and goats eat grass and leaves; parrots eat fruits and seeds.
Bees and butterflies drink nectar from flowers.
Plants give animals shelter. Birds build nests in trees, and squirrels live in tree holes.
Even a tiger needs plants! It eats deer, and deer eat grass and leaves.
We humans also get food, wood and cloth (cotton) from plants.

ex.q: A tiger never eats grass. Does it still depend on plants?
st: A tiger eats animals like deer.
Deer eat grass and leaves to live.
Without plants there would be no deer, so the tiger would have no food.
ex.a: Yes. The tiger eats deer, and deer depend on plants for food.

topics.rl: Look at the trees near your home. Can you spot a nest, a squirrel or ants climbing up the trunk?

rv.summary: Many animals depend on plants for food and shelter. Even meat-eaters like tigers depend on plants, because the animals they eat feed on plants. People also get food, wood and cotton from plants.
focus: How meat-eaters still depend on plants
remember: Cows and goats eat grass and leaves; parrots eat fruits and seeds
Bees and butterflies drink nectar
Birds nest in trees; squirrels live in tree holes
Plants make their own food; animals cannot
traps: Don't think a tiger does not need plants; its food (deer) eats plants.
Glass, iron and plastic do not come from plants.

topics.h: Plants help animals, but did you know animals help plants too? It is a two-way friendship!
p: When bees and butterflies visit flowers, they carry a yellow powder called pollen from flower to flower. This helps flowers make fruits and seeds.
Birds and animals eat fruits and drop the seeds far away, where new plants can grow.
Some seeds have tiny hooks that stick to animal fur and travel with them.
Earthworms dig in the soil and make it soft and airy, which helps roots grow.
Cow dung is used as manure that makes the soil rich for plants.

ex.q: A farmer in Himachal keeps bee boxes in his apple orchard. Why might he do this?
st: Bees visit apple flowers for nectar.
While doing this, they carry pollen between flowers.
This helps the flowers turn into apples, so the farmer gets more fruit.
ex.a: The bees help the apple flowers make fruit

topics.rl: Earthworms in your garden soil are tiny helpers. Never harm them — they keep the soil healthy!

rv.summary: Animals help plants too: bees and butterflies carry pollen, birds and animals spread seeds, earthworms make soil soft and airy, and cow dung manure makes soil rich.
focus: How bees and butterflies help flowers
How earthworms and manure help soil
remember: Pollen = yellow powder carried from flower to flower
Birds drop seeds far away; hooked seeds stick to fur
Earthworms make the soil soft and airy
Cow dung manure makes soil rich
traps: A cow eating grass is a plant helping an animal, not an animal helping a plant.

topics.h: A fish cannot live in a desert, and a camel cannot live in the sea. Why? Every living thing has its own home!
p: A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, where it finds food, water and shelter.
Some habitats are on land, like forests, deserts and mountains. Others are in water, like ponds, rivers and the sea.
Camels live in deserts. Their wide, padded feet help them walk on sand, and they can go many days without water.
Yaks live in cold mountains like Ladakh. Their thick, long hair keeps them warm.
Fish breathe in water using gills. The cactus stores water in its thick stem to live in the desert. The lotus grows in ponds.

ex.q: Why does a camel not sink into the desert sand like we do?
st: Think about the camel's feet.
They are wide and padded, so its weight spreads out.
This stops its feet from sinking deep into soft sand.
ex.a: Its wide, padded feet help it walk on soft sand without sinking

topics.rl: On a trip, look at the plants and animals around you. A beach, a hill station and a desert all have different living things!

rv.summary: A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, on land or in water. Living things suit their homes, like camels in deserts, yaks in cold mountains, fish in water and cactus in deserts.
focus: How camels, yaks, fish, cactus and lotus suit their homes
remember: Habitat = natural home with food, water and shelter
Camel: padded feet, hump stores fat
Yak: thick, long hair for cold mountains
Fish breathe with gills; cactus stores water in its stem
traps: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
Fish breathe with gills, not with a nose.

topics.h: A tiny ant, a street dog, a big banyan tree — they all share the Earth with us!
p: All living beings — people, animals and plants — need food, water and a safe place to live.
We should never hurt, tease or throw stones at animals.
In summer, we can keep a bowl of water out for birds and street animals.
We should not break branches or pluck flowers and leaves for no reason.
Every creature has a job in nature. Even spiders and earthworms are helpful.

ex.q: Some boys are throwing stones at a street puppy. What should Priya do?
st: Think: the puppy can get hurt and feel scared, just like us.
Priya should not join in, and should ask the boys to stop.
She should tell a trusted adult, who can help the puppy.
ex.a: Ask them to stop and tell a trusted adult

topics.rl: Many children in India keep clay bowls of water on balconies in summer for sparrows, pigeons and mynas.

rv.summary: All living beings need food, water and a safe home. We should be kind to animals and plants, never hurt them, give water to birds in summer, and remember every creature is useful.
focus: India's national bird, animal and tree
remember: Never hurt, tease or throw stones at animals
Keep water out for birds and street animals in summer
National bird: peacock; national animal: tiger; national tree: banyan
Spiders and earthworms are helpful
traps: The lion is not India's national animal; the tiger is.
Don't carry an injured bird yourself; tell an adult.

topics.h: Trees, rivers, birds and bees keep the Earth beautiful. How can we keep nature safe?
p: Nature gives us air, water, food, wood and medicines.
We protect nature by planting trees, not wasting water and not littering.
In the Chipko movement in the hills of Uttarakhand, villagers hugged trees to stop them from being cut.
The Bishnoi people of Rajasthan are known for protecting khejri trees and blackbucks.
World Environment Day is on 5 June. Van Mahotsav, a tree-planting festival, is held in the first week of July.

ex.q: Why did the villagers in the Chipko movement hug the trees?
st: The trees were going to be cut down.
The villagers needed the forest for wood, food, water and fodder.
By hugging the trees, they stopped the axes and saved the forest.
ex.a: To stop the trees from being cut and to save their forest

topics.rl: Plant a sapling with your family and give it a name. Water it and watch it grow with you!

rv.summary: Nature gives us air, water, food, wood and medicines, so we protect it by planting trees, saving water and not littering. The Chipko movement and the Bishnoi people are famous for protecting nature.
focus: Special days: World Environment Day, Van Mahotsav
remember: Chipko: villagers in Uttarakhand hugged trees to save them
Bishnoi people of Rajasthan protect khejri trees and blackbucks
World Environment Day = 5 June
Van Mahotsav = first week of July
traps: Don't mix up the dates: World Environment Day is 5 June, not 15 August.
Never throw garbage into rivers or lakes.

topics.h: Where does the water in your tap come from? Let's follow it back to where it started!
p: Rain is the main source of fresh water. Rainwater fills rivers, lakes, ponds and wells.
Some rainwater soaks into the ground. We draw this groundwater using wells, hand pumps and borewells.
Snow on high mountains melts and flows into rivers. The Ganga starts from the Gangotri glacier in the Himalayas.
Sea water is salty, so we cannot drink it or use it to water crops.
Long ago, people built stepwells (baoris or vavs) to store water, like the Rani ki Vav in Gujarat and Chand Baori in Rajasthan.

ex.q: There is plenty of water in the sea. Why can't the people of Chennai simply drink sea water?
st: Sea water tastes very salty.
Salty water is not safe for drinking.
So fresh water from rain, rivers, lakes and the ground is needed for drinking.
ex.a: Sea water is too salty to drink

topics.rl: Find out where your home's water comes from — a river, a lake, a well or a borewell. Ask an elder!

rv.summary: Rain is the main source of fresh water. It fills rivers, lakes, ponds and wells and soaks into the ground as groundwater. Melting snow feeds rivers like the Ganga. Sea water is too salty to drink.
focus: Groundwater and how we draw it
remember: Rain = main source of fresh water
Groundwater is drawn by wells, hand pumps and borewells
The Ganga starts at the Gangotri glacier
Stepwells: Rani ki Vav (Gujarat), Chand Baori (Rajasthan)
traps: The sea is not a source of drinking water; it is salty.
Taps are not the source of water; they only bring it to us.

topics.h: Count how many times you use water today. You may be surprised!
p: We need water to drink, cook, bathe, brush our teeth and wash clothes and dishes.
Farmers need water to grow crops. Plants cannot live without water.
Animals need water to drink, and fish and lotus live in water.
Boats carry people and goods on rivers and seas.
Drinking water must be clean. Boiling or filtering water makes it safe to drink.

ex.q: Raju's family boils drinking water and lets it cool before drinking. Why?
st: Water may look clean but can still have tiny germs.
Germs can make us sick with stomach problems.
Boiling kills these germs, so the water becomes safe.
ex.a: Boiling kills germs and makes the water safe to drink

topics.rl: Keep your water bottle clean and covered. Drink water often, especially on hot days.

rv.summary: We use water to drink, cook, bathe and clean. Farmers need it for crops, animals need it to drink, and boats travel on it. Drinking water must be clean, covered, and boiled or filtered.
focus: Uses of water at home, on farms and for animals
remember: Rice is often grown in fields with standing water
Boiling or filtering makes water safe to drink
Keep drinking water covered
Dirty water can cause stomach illnesses
traps: Water that looks clear may still have germs; boil or filter it.
Never leave drinking water uncovered.

topics.h: Fresh water is precious. Only a small part of all the water on Earth is fresh and fit to drink!
p: Most of Earth's water is salty sea water. Fresh water is limited, so we must not waste it.
Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth or soaping your hands.
Use a bucket and mug for bathing instead of letting water run.
Get leaking taps fixed. Reuse water used for washing vegetables to water plants.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainwater for later use.

ex.q: Aryan leaves the tap running while he brushes his teeth. What should he do, and why?
st: Water flows away and is wasted while the tap runs.
He can fill a mug of water and turn the tap off.
This saves fresh water, which is limited.
ex.a: Turn off the tap while brushing and use a mug, to save water

topics.rl: World Water Day is on 22 March. Make a 'Save Water' poster for your school that day!

rv.summary: Fresh water is limited, so we must not waste it. Turn off taps, use a bucket and mug, fix leaks, reuse water for plants, and collect rainwater.
remember: Turn off the tap while brushing or soaping
Bucket-and-mug bath saves water
Rainwater harvesting = collecting and storing rainwater
World Water Day = 22 March
traps: Don't think there is plenty of fresh water; most water on Earth is salty.
Water from washing vegetables is for plants, not for drinking.

topics.h: Roti, dal, rice, sabzi, curd... Where does all this food come from?
p: We get food from plants and from animals.
From plants we get cereals (rice, wheat), millets (ragi, jowar, bajra), pulses (dal), fruits, vegetables and oils.
From animals we get milk, curd, paneer, eggs, honey, fish and meat.
Some families eat only plant foods and milk. Others also eat eggs, fish or meat. All these are choices families make.
Millets are healthy grains grown in India. The year 2023 was celebrated as the International Year of Millets.

ex.q: Paneer is white and soft. Does it come from a plant or an animal?
st: Paneer is made by curdling milk.
Milk comes from animals like cows and buffaloes.
So paneer is a food we get from animals.
ex.a: From an animal (it is made from milk)

topics.rl: At your next meal, look at your plate and sort each item: did it come from a plant or an animal?

rv.summary: We get food from plants (cereals, millets, pulses, fruits, vegetables, oils) and from animals (milk, curd, paneer, eggs, honey, fish, meat). Millets are healthy grains grown in India.
focus: Sorting foods into plant foods and animal foods
remember: Cereals: rice, wheat; millets: ragi, jowar, bajra; pulses: dal
Animal foods: milk, curd, paneer, eggs, honey, fish, meat
Bees make honey; curd and paneer are made from milk
2023 = International Year of Millets
traps: Paneer comes from an animal (milk), not a plant.
Peanuts come from a plant, not an animal.

topics.h: A potato can be boiled, fried, roasted or baked. One food, so many tastes!
p: Some foods are eaten raw, like fruits, cucumbers and carrots in a salad.
Boiling: cooking in hot bubbling water, like rice, dal and eggs.
Frying: cooking in hot oil, like puris, pakoras and samosas.
Steaming: cooking with steam from boiling water, like idlis, dhoklas and modaks.
Roasting cooks food over a flame, like bhutta, and baking cooks food in an oven, like bread and cake. Cooking is always done by or with an adult!

ex.q: Idli batter is poured into moulds and kept over boiling water in a closed pot. The idlis never touch the water. How are they cooked?
st: The food does not sit in the water, so it is not boiled.
There is no oil, so it is not fried.
The hot steam rising from the water cooks the idlis. This is steaming.
ex.a: By steaming

topics.rl: Watch an adult cook at home and name the cooking method used for each dish. Never use the stove on your own.

rv.summary: Some foods are eaten raw, and others are cooked by boiling, frying, steaming, roasting or baking. Cooking is always done by or with an adult.
focus: Foods eaten raw and washing them
remember: Boiling: rice, dal, eggs
Frying: puris, pakoras, samosas
Steaming: idli, dhokla, modak
Roasting: bhutta; baking: bread, cake
traps: Idli and dhokla are steamed, not fried or boiled.
Children should not use the stove on their own.

topics.h: Travel across India on a plate! Every state has its own yummy dishes.
p: People in different parts of India eat different foods, based on what grows there and their customs.
In many parts of north India, wheat rotis are common. In many parts of south and east India, rice is eaten more.
Punjab: makki di roti with sarson da saag. Gujarat: dhokla. Rajasthan: dal baati churma. Bihar: litti chokha.
Tamil Nadu: idli and dosa. Kerala: puttu and appam. Maharashtra: puran poli and vada pav.
People living near the sea, like in Goa and Kerala, often eat fish and use coconut in cooking.

ex.q: Why do many dishes in Kerala use coconut?
st: Kerala lies along the sea coast.
Coconut trees grow in large numbers there.
Food that grows nearby is used often in local cooking.
ex.a: Because a lot of coconut trees grow in Kerala

topics.rl: Ask a friend from another state about a favourite dish from home. Maybe you can share tiffins!

rv.summary: People in different parts of India eat different foods, based on what grows there and their customs. Wheat rotis are common in the north, rice in the south and east, and fish and coconut near the sea.
focus: Why foods differ from place to place
remember: Punjab: makki di roti and sarson da saag; Gujarat: dhokla
Rajasthan: dal baati churma; Bihar: litti chokha
Tamil Nadu: idli, dosa; Kerala: puttu, appam; Maharashtra: puran poli, vada pav
Coastal places like Goa and Kerala use fish and coconut
traps: Don't mix up states: dhokla is Gujarat, puttu is Kerala.
Food is not the same everywhere; it depends on local crops and customs.

topics.h: Germs are too tiny to see, but they can make us sick. Let's beat them with clean habits!
p: Hygiene means keeping our body and surroundings clean so we stay healthy.
Wash your hands with soap and water before eating and after using the toilet. Rub for about 20 seconds.
Brush your teeth twice a day — in the morning and before going to bed.
Bathe every day, wear clean clothes and keep your nails short and clean.
Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow when you cough or sneeze.

ex.q: Kavya played in the mud and now wants to eat a banana. Her hands look only a little dirty. What should she do first?
st: Germs are too small to see, so hands can carry germs even if they look clean.
Germs on hands can go into the mouth with food.
So she should wash her hands with soap and water before eating.
ex.a: Wash her hands with soap and water before eating

topics.rl: Hum 'Happy Birthday' twice while you rub your hands with soap. That is about 20 seconds!

rv.summary: Hygiene means keeping our body and surroundings clean. Wash hands with soap, brush twice a day, bathe daily, keep nails short, and cover coughs and sneezes.
focus: When and how to wash hands
remember: Wash hands with soap before eating and after the toilet, for about 20 seconds
Brush teeth twice a day
Keep nails short and clean
Cover mouth and nose with a tissue or elbow when sneezing
traps: Hands that look a little dirty still need washing before eating.
Food that falls on a dirty floor is not safe to eat.

topics.h: Run, jump, stretch, then sleep tight! Your body needs both play and rest.
p: Exercise makes our muscles and bones strong and keeps the heart healthy.
Children should be active for at least an hour every day — running, cycling, dancing, skipping or playing kho-kho and kabaddi.
Yoga helps the body bend and stay calm. International Day of Yoga is on 21 June.
Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep every night.
Too much time on phones and TV can tire the eyes. Playing outdoors is better.

ex.q: Sameer stays up very late watching cartoons and feels sleepy in class. What should he change?
st: Sleep helps the body and brain rest and grow.
Children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep.
He should switch off the TV earlier and go to bed on time.
ex.a: Turn off the TV early and go to bed on time to get enough sleep

topics.rl: Play a game of kho-kho, langdi or hopscotch with your friends this evening!

rv.summary: Exercise makes muscles, bones and the heart strong. Children should be active at least an hour a day, sleep about 9 to 12 hours, and spend less time on screens.
focus: How much activity and sleep children need
Yoga and International Day of Yoga
remember: Be active for at least an hour every day
Sleep about 9 to 12 hours every night
International Day of Yoga = 21 June
Rest helps the body get back its energy
traps: Rest is not a waste of time; the body recovers and grows then.
Watching TV for hours is not exercise.

topics.h: Is a plate of only chips a good lunch? Let's find out what a healthy plate looks like!
p: A balanced meal has the right mix of different foods that our body needs.
Energy-giving foods: rice, roti, millets and potatoes give us energy to work and play.
Body-building foods: dal, milk, paneer, eggs and fish help us grow strong.
Protective foods: fruits and vegetables help keep us healthy.
Drink plenty of clean water. Eat chips, sweets and cold drinks only once in a while.

ex.q: Meera's lunch is only rice. What can she add to make it a balanced meal?
st: Rice gives energy, but it does not have everything.
She needs body-building food like dal or curd.
She also needs protective food like a vegetable or a fruit.
ex.a: Add dal or curd and a vegetable or fruit

topics.rl: Make your thali colourful: something white, something yellow, something green — that usually means a good mix!

rv.summary: A balanced meal has the right mix of energy-giving, body-building and protective foods, with plenty of clean water. Junk food is only for once in a while.
focus: Three kinds of food and their examples
remember: Energy-giving: rice, roti, millets, potatoes
Body-building: dal, milk, paneer, eggs, fish
Protective: fruits and vegetables
Clean water is the best drink
traps: A meal of only rice is not balanced; add dal or curd and a vegetable or fruit.
Don't mix up dal (body-building) with roti (energy-giving).

topics.h: Look around you. Which things did nature make, and which did people make?
p: Natural things are found in nature. People do not make them — like the sun, air, water, soil, stones and trees.
Human-made things are made by people — like chairs, pencils, buckets, bicycles and clothes.
Human-made things are made from natural things. Paper is made from wood, glass from sand, and cotton cloth from the cotton plant.
Wool comes from sheep, and silk comes from silkworms.
A tree is natural, but a wooden chair made from it is human-made.

ex.q: Is a clay matka natural or human-made?
st: Clay is found in nature, so clay is natural.
But a potter shaped the clay and baked it into a matka.
So the matka is a human-made thing made from a natural material.
ex.a: Human-made (made by a potter from natural clay)

topics.rl: Go on a 'things hunt' at home. List 5 natural things and 5 human-made things you can see.

rv.summary: Natural things are found in nature, like air, water, soil and trees. Human-made things are made by people from natural things, like paper from wood and glass from sand.
focus: Telling natural things from human-made things
Which natural thing each material comes from
Materials from animals: wool and silk
remember: Paper from wood; glass from sand; cotton cloth from the cotton plant
Wool from sheep; silk from silkworms
A tree is natural, but a wooden chair is human-made
traps: A wooden table is human-made even though wood is natural.
Wool and silk come from animals, not plants.

topics.h: A spoon can be steel, plastic or wood. What things are made of is called their material!
p: The stuff a thing is made of is its material. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, clay, paper, cloth and rubber are materials.
One thing can be made of different materials: a cup can be made of steel, glass, clay or plastic.
Many things use more than one material: a pencil has wood and graphite, and a pan has metal and a plastic handle.
We choose a material that suits the job: steel for spoons, rubber for tyres, glass for windows.
Metals like iron, steel, copper and aluminium are hard and often shiny.

ex.q: Why are cooking pans made of metal but their handles made of plastic or wood?
st: Metal lets heat pass through quickly, so the food cooks.
Plastic and wood do not let heat pass through easily.
So the handle stays cool enough to hold.
ex.a: Metal heats the food quickly, while a plastic or wooden handle stays cool to hold

topics.rl: In the kitchen, spot things made of steel, glass, plastic and clay. Ask an adult before touching anything hot.

rv.summary: A material is the stuff a thing is made of. One thing can be made of different materials, many things use more than one, and we choose a material that suits the job.

Things made of more than one material

Rubber for tyres; glass for windows; steel for spoons
Pencil = wood + graphite; pan = metal + plastic handle
Metals: iron, steel, copper, aluminium
traps: Pan handles are plastic or wood because they do not get hot quickly, not to look nice.
Glass is not soft or bendy.

topics.h: Why is a raincoat not made of paper? Because every material behaves in its own way!
p: Some materials are hard, like stone and metal. Some are soft, like cotton and wool.
Glass and clear plastic are see-through. Wood and metal are not.
Some materials soak up water, like a towel or a sponge. Others keep water out, like a plastic raincoat or a rubber boot.
Rubber bands stretch and go back. Glass and clay pots can break easily if dropped.
In water, things like a cork or a dry leaf float, while a coin or a pebble sinks.

ex.q: Arjun wants to wipe up spilt water. Should he use a plastic sheet or a cotton cloth?
st: Plastic does not soak up water. It just pushes the water around.
Cotton cloth soaks up water.
So the cotton cloth will wipe up the spill.
ex.a: A cotton cloth, because it soaks up water

topics.rl: Do a float-or-sink test in a bucket of water at home with an adult: try a coin, a cork, a leaf and a plastic lid.

rv.summary: Materials have different properties: hard or soft, see-through or not, soak up water or keep it out, stretch or break, float or sink.
focus: Materials that soak up or keep out water
remember: Hard: stone, metal; soft: cotton, wool
See-through: glass, clear plastic
Soak water: towel, sponge; keep water out: plastic raincoat, rubber boot
Float: cork, dry leaf; sink: coin, pebble
traps: Small things do not always float; a coin sinks.
Glass is hard but breaks easily.

topics.h: Who made your clay diya, your wooden stool and your cotton kurta? Skilled hands called artisans!
p: Artisans are skilled people who make things with their hands and simple tools.
A potter shapes clay on a spinning wheel called a chaak to make pots, diyas and matkas.
A weaver makes cloth on a loom. A carpenter makes furniture from wood.
A blacksmith heats iron till it glows and beats it into tools. A basket maker weaves baskets from bamboo or cane.
Artisans often learn their skills from elders in the family, and they take great care over each piece.

ex.q: A potter has wet clay. Why does he dry the pot in the sun and then bake it in a hot kiln?
st: Wet clay is soft, so the pot can lose its shape or break.
Drying in the sun removes water from the clay.
Baking it in a kiln makes the pot hard and strong so it can hold water.
ex.a: Drying and baking make the clay pot hard and strong

topics.rl: Next time you buy diyas or a matka, remember the potter who made each one by hand.

rv.summary: Artisans are skilled people who make things by hand with simple tools, like potters, weavers, carpenters, blacksmiths and basket makers. They often learn from elders.
focus: Matching artisans to what they make
remember: Potter: clay on a chaak, pots baked in a kiln
Weaver: cloth on a loom; carpenter: wood
Blacksmith: heats and beats iron into tools
Basket maker: bamboo or cane
traps: Chaak is the potter's wheel; charkha is for spinning thread.
Baking makes clay hard, not soft.

topics.h: India has hundreds of crafts! Each region has its own colours, patterns and styles.
p: Madhubani paintings from Bihar are full of bright colours, fish, birds and flowers.
Warli paintings from Maharashtra use simple white shapes like circles, triangles and lines.
Blue pottery comes from Jaipur in Rajasthan. Bandhani, a tie-and-dye cloth, is made in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Channapatna in Karnataka is famous for colourful wooden toys. Kondapalli in Andhra Pradesh makes wooden toys too.
Pashmina shawls come from Kashmir. Bamboo and cane crafts are famous in Assam and other states of the North-East.

ex.q: A painting shows people dancing in a circle, drawn using only white triangles, circles and lines. Which painting style is this likely to be?
st: The clues are: simple shapes and white colour.
Warli painting uses white shapes like circles, triangles and lines.
So this is most likely a Warli painting.
ex.a: Warli painting

topics.rl: Look at the dupattas, toys or pots in your home. Can you find out which state's craft they are?

rv.summary: India has many famous crafts from different states, like Madhubani from Bihar, Warli from Maharashtra, blue pottery from Jaipur, Channapatna toys from Karnataka and pashmina from Kashmir.
remember: Madhubani – Bihar; Warli (white shapes) – Maharashtra; Pattachitra – Odisha
Blue pottery – Jaipur; bandhani (tie-and-dye) – Gujarat and Rajasthan
Channapatna toys – Karnataka; Kondapalli toys – Andhra Pradesh
Pashmina – Kashmir; bamboo and cane – Assam and the North-East
traps: Don't mix up Madhubani (bright, Bihar) with Warli (white shapes, Maharashtra).
Blue pottery is from Jaipur, not Chennai.

topics.h: An old bottle, a used box, a torn T-shirt — don't throw them away. Turn them into treasure!
p: Many things we throw away can be used again to make something new and useful.
An empty plastic bottle can become a plant pot or a bird feeder.
Old newspapers can be folded into paper bags.
Old clothes can be cut into strips and woven into a doormat or a rag doll.
Always ask an adult to help with scissors or sharp edges, and wash containers clean before using them.

ex.q: Ishaan has an empty plastic bottle, some string and grains. What useful thing can he make?
st: A bottle can hold grains.
With an adult's help, small holes can be cut in the side for birds to peck through.
Hang it from a branch with string.
ex.a: A bird feeder

topics.rl: Make a 'best out of waste' corner at home or school. See how many useful things your class can make!

rv.summary: Many things we throw away can be made into new, useful things, like bottle plant pots, newspaper bags and cloth doormats. Always ask an adult for help with sharp things and wash containers first.
remember: Plastic bottle → plant pot or bird feeder
Old newspapers → paper bags
Old clothes → doormat or rag doll
Ask an adult for scissors or sharp edges; wash containers first
traps: Never use broken glass for crafts.
Don't cut tins or bottles alone.

topics.h: Banana peels, chips packets, old newspapers... Is all garbage the same? No way!
p: Waste is anything we throw away because we do not need it any more.
Wet waste comes from plants and food, like peels, leftover food, tea leaves and fallen leaves. It rots and mixes with the soil.
Dry waste includes paper, plastic, glass, metal and old cloth. Most of it does not rot quickly.
Plastic does not rot. It can stay in the soil and water for a very, very long time.
Some waste, like old batteries, medicines and broken bulbs, is harmful and must be handed over carefully by an adult.

ex.q: A banana peel and a plastic wrapper are left in the garden for many weeks. What happens to each?
st: The banana peel comes from a plant. Tiny living things break it down.
It slowly rots and mixes with the soil.
The plastic wrapper does not rot. It stays almost the same for years.
ex.a: The peel rots and mixes with soil; the plastic wrapper stays as it is

topics.rl: Look at your kitchen dustbin after dinner. How much of it is wet waste and how much is dry?

rv.summary: Waste is what we throw away. Wet waste from food and plants rots and mixes with soil; dry waste like paper, plastic, glass and metal does not rot quickly. Plastic does not rot, and some waste is harmful.
focus: What happens to peels and plastic over time
Harmful waste and why not to burn garbage
remember: Wet waste: peels, leftover food, tea leaves, fallen leaves
Dry waste: paper, plastic, glass, metal, old cloth
Plastic does not rot
Batteries, medicines and broken bulbs must be handed over by an adult
traps: Paper is dry waste even though it comes from trees.
Burning garbage is not a good way to get rid of it; the smoke is harmful.

topics.h: Two bins can save the Earth a lot of trouble! Let's learn to sort our waste.
p: Keep wet waste and dry waste in separate bins at home and school.
In many cities, the green bin is for wet waste and the blue bin is for dry waste.
Sorted wet waste can be turned into compost, a rich manure for plants.
To make compost, put wet waste in a pit or a pot, cover it with soil or dry leaves, and wait some weeks.
Earthworms and tiny living things break the waste down into compost.

ex.q: Why is it a good idea to keep wet and dry waste in separate bins?
st: Wet waste can be turned into compost.
Dry waste like paper, glass and metal can be sent for recycling.
If they are mixed, the wet waste makes the dry waste dirty and both become hard to use.
ex.a: So wet waste can become compost and dry waste can be recycled

topics.rl: Help your family keep two bins in the kitchen — one for wet waste and one for dry waste.

topics.h: Three magic words can shrink a mountain of garbage: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle!
p: Reduce means using fewer things so less waste is made, like carrying a cloth bag instead of taking plastic bags.
Reuse means using things again, like using a jam jar to store buttons.
Recycle means turning old things into new things. Old paper becomes new paper; old glass becomes new glass.
The kabadiwala buys old newspapers, bottles and metal and sends them for recycling.
Carry a steel water bottle and a tiffin box, and say no to single-use plastic.

ex.q: Ananya's mother takes the same cloth bag to the vegetable market every day. How does this help cut down waste?
st: She uses the same bag again and again — that is reusing the bag.
Because of this, she does not need new plastic bags, so less waste is made.
Not taking plastic bags means she is reducing waste.
ex.a: She reuses one cloth bag, so no new plastic bags end up as waste. This reduces waste.

topics.rl: Count the plastic bags that come home in a week. Can your family bring that number down?

rv.summary: Reduce means using fewer things, reuse means using things again, and recycle means turning old things into new ones. The kabadiwala helps by sending old things for recycling.
